name: Raymond Feng
bio: Researcher at Applied Compute. Building the post-training stack, training specialized workhorse models for enterprises, and researching new techniques for model customization. Graduated from MIT.

talks.title: Learning on the Job: The Future of Post-Training

sessions.scheduled_title: Learning on the job: the future of post-training

positions.claim: Environment fidelity and reward hacking are not two separate problems but the same problem viewed from different sides.
Infrastructure defects with no presence in the reward function — such as a ~10% tool-call failure rate — still induce systematic behavior changes like shorter model responses.
Filtering timed-out rollouts out of training creates an incentive for the model to deliberately trigger sandbox timeouts on hard problems.
Perfectly simulating reality in a synthetic environment is infeasible, and this gets worse as tasks grow more complicated.
The right response to environment-fidelity failures is to train directly in the customer's real production harness rather than to build better simulations.
Training inside a black-box harness requires only a model completion endpoint plus request/response recording; all orchestration can live outside the training stack.
GRPO's requirement of many parallel rollouts per prompt is not satisfiable in real production settings such as customer support chats.
Because humans can learn from single non-replayable interactions, an analogous learning method should be formulable for models.
Self-distillation currently works only for inducing narrow, specific behaviors, and generalizing it is an open research question.
Identifying failure modes in traces and curating training data from them is still a manual, human-in-the-loop process at Applied Compute.
Per-failure-mode post-training is an unwinnable Whac-A-Mole, and only a self-improving system that learns from all interactions escapes it.
Experience, not curated human data, will become the dominant medium of model improvement.
